## PAGE 1

**Strong Predictors, Weak Selectors:
Why Confidence Signals Fail to Scale Structured Information Extraction**

Anonymous ACL submission

---

**Abstract**

Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces sets of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists. We evaluate five confidence signals, four instance-level (structural and surface agreement) and one per-sample (log-probability), for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient (SciERC, Few-NERD, CoNLL, WNUT17), using 40-98 models. All signals achieve reliable quality estimation (ρ up to 0.42 on Few-NERD and the primary test bed; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging. However, quality estimation does not translate to structural selection, the correlation-selection gap: structural best-of-N selection matches or degrades greedy decoding (T=0) despite 12-14 pp oracle headroom. We diagnose two mechanisms: (a) instance degeneracy, fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 10-58% of instances, eliminating selection headroom, and (b) log-probability compression, median within-instance range of 0.041 nats. LP selection effectiveness is inversely predicted by degeneracy; at 10% degeneracy LP achieves +1.36 pp (p<0.001), at 29% (SciERC), +0.12 pp (n.s) 0.85 (CoNLL, 83% LP falls. Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, confirming the gap is persistent for consensus-based methods. Closing the structural gap likely requires learned per-sample scoring.

---

**1 Introduction**

Self-consistency, majority voting over multiple samples, yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning (Wang et al., 2023), and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling (Snell et al., 2025; Brown et al., 2024). But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a

set of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated quality estimation (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with sample selection (which of N outputs is best?). Existing self-consistency methods (Wang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Taucherdzhiev et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025) assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap. Yao et al. (2026) study consistency-accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE using exact-match agreement under hard-prompting; we extend their work to fine-tuned models, separating quality estimation from best-of-N selection and diagnosing why the former succeeds while the latter fails, within the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER.

A methodological premise structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that by design assign identical score to all N candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample. These signals achieve reliable quality estimation (ρ up to 0.42 on the primary test bed and Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82; Figure 1), supporting selective prediction and error flagging. Yet quality estimation does not translate to structural selection, the **correlation-selection gap**: structural best-of-N selection matches or degrades greedy decoding (T=0) despite 12-14 pp oracle headroom. The gap has two empirical causes: (a) instance degeneracy, fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 10-58% of instances, eliminating selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility-F1 correlation (median ρ=0.52); and (b) LP compression, median within-instance range of 0.041 nats (§5). LP selection is degeneracy-gated: significant at 10% degeneracy (+1.36 pp, p<0.001), sub-significant at 29%

---

## PAGE 2

(+0.12 pp), and absent at 58%.

We evaluate five signals from three families, structural, surface, and model-internal, on SciERC (Luan et al., 2018) as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD (Ding et al., 2021) (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 (Sang and Meulder, 2003) (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 (Derczynski et al., 2017) (signal collapse boundary), using two 98 models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B). An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix L. Our contributions:

1. **Quality estimation framework.** We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families, structural, surface, and model-internal, for LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient. Structural signals reliably predict output quality (MC ρ=0.38 on the primary test bed; LM AUROC=0.83 on CoNLL), with difficulty-dependent but model-stable rankings that support selective prediction and error flagging.

2. **Diagnosis of the correlation-selection gap.** Quality estimation does not translate to structural selection; despite 12-14 pp oracle headroom, no structural signal significantly outperforms greedy decoding on any dataset (p>0.05), a gap confirmed by bootstrap testing at N=32. We trace this to two mechanisms, instance degeneracy (10-58% of instances yield identical outputs, colliding with model capability) and LP compression (median within-instance range 0.041 nats) and confirm via a diagnostic chain (LoRA-rank ablation, free-form decoding, entity-token LP, supervised signal combination) that the structural bottleneck lies in the feature space, not signal aggregation or decoding constraints. LP selection effectiveness is inversely predicted by degeneracy rate across three datasets (58% → fail, 29% → +0.12 pp, 10% → +1.36 pp at p<0.001), establishing degeneracy as a predictive mechanism for selection viability.

**2 Related Work**

**Self-consistency and test-time scaling.** Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text through LLM comparison (Chen et al.,

2024), sub-claim decomposition (Thirukovalluru et al., 2024), or hallucination detection (Manakul et al., 2023). Test-time scaling studies (Snell et al., 2025; Brown et al., 2024) and reward-free selectors (Taubenfeld et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Oh and Lee, 2026) all rely on answer-level agreement signals that assume equivalence can be determined via exact match or semantic similarity. Concurrently, Feng et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2025b) adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings. Li et al. (2025) propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on fusion rather than selection. Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap.

**Consistency for structured IE.** Yao et al. (2026) study consistency-accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE under hard-prompting, leaving open whether structural matching improves on surface agreement, whether quality estimation translates to selection, and whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient, the three questions we address. Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, where instance degeneracy is most pronounced. Degeneracy varies across datasets: CoNLL (91% single-sample F1) exhibits 58%; SciERC (66%) shows 21%; Few-NERD (75%) shows 10%. WNUT17 (T=0.25), macro shows near zero (§5). Few-NERD's low degeneracy despite high performance reveals that dataset-specific factors modulate degeneracy beyond model capability alone. CoCo-A (Vashisth et al., 2025) fuses confidence with consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction; our supervised verifier baseline (logistic regression on all five signals, no oracle gap closure; §4.5) confirms that the combination strategy itself is not the bottleneck. Colubin and McCallum (2006) and Major and Cranmer (2010) pioneer confidence estimation for structured prediction via CRF marginals and confidence-weighted models. Fomicheva et al. (2020) systematically apply model-internal signals (MC Dropout, D-Lex) for unsupervised quality estimation in NMT, establishing the paradigm we extend from sequence-level to set-valued structured outputs. Our evaluation builds on generative IE work (Chen et al., 2024; Sainz et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Wadhwa et al., 2023) and constrained decoding (Willard and Louf, 2023; Park et al., 2024); recent work highlights hidden costs of constrained

generation for log-probability estimation (Schall and de Melo, 2025) and inference efficiency (Yun et al., 2025).

**Uncertainty estimation and calibration.** Surveys cover confidence estimation (Geng et al., 2024), uncertainty quantification (Xu et al., 2025), and calibration (Hobbesheidler et al., 2025) for LLMs. Semantic uncertainty (Kuhn et al., 2023) quotes model confidence directly; Malinin and Gales (2021) study predictive uncertainty for autoregressive structured prediction. Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output structure, requiring no model modification. Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding (Eikema and Aziz, 2022; Deguchi et al., 2024) with structural utility functions. Unlike machine translation where MBR yields consistent gains (Freitag et al., 2022), we find that utility is aligned with quality (within-instance SJ-F1 ρ=0.52) but instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that would otherwise exploit. Eikema et al. (2025) find that standard MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs due to bag-of-unit mismatches; our diagnosis is complementary, the bottleneck is not utility misalignment but output concentration driven by model capability (§5). Xie et al. (2024) show self-evaluation improves selective generation for discrete tasks; our results suggest this does not transfer to structured extraction without learned scoring. Our quality estimation results connect to selective

prediction (Kalenkov and Liang, 2015): signals with ρ up to 0.45 on CoNLL (0.42 on the primary test bed) and AUROC up to 0.82 can support abstention policies that flag low-quality extractions, providing practical value independent of sample selection. Conditional prediction constructs prediction sets with coverage guarantees (Zhang et al., 2025); while complementary, its set-valued output differs from best-of-N selection.

**Best-of-N with learned verifiers.** Gao et al. (2023) establish scaling laws for best-of-N selection with learned reward models, showing that BoN performance scales log-linearly with N but eventually degrades due to reward overoptimization. Our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation: they cannot rank candidates at all (instance-level signals) or rank them too weakly (LP compression), making the overoptimization regime irrelevant. Trained verifiers (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) and quality-aware decoding (Fernandes et al., 2022) learn per-sample scoring that may bridge this gap; our LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7% vs. 21%, selection still fails) suggests that verifier training is necessary beyond merely increasing output diversity. Fine-tuning itself contributes to the problem: Kirk et al. (2024) document diversity collapse in RLHF-trained models; our instance degeneracy is an analogous phenomenon in supervised fine-tuning, where stronger models converge to more uniform outputs. Nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2020) improves diversity in open-

---

## PAGE 4

ended generation, but our constrained structured outputs limit the diversity that temperature scaling alone can recover.

**3 Method**

**3.1 Problem Formulation**

Given model M and input x, we sample N outputs y₁, ..., y_N at temperature T > 0 via constrained decoding (Willard and Louf, 2023), where each y_i is an entity set. A **per-sample** signal σ_ps(x_j, y_j) → ℝ scores each output independently; an **instance-level** signal σ_il = f({y₁, ..., y_N}) → ℝ produces a single score per input (notation in Appendix A). This distinction is consequential for selection: in our study, 4 of 5 signals are instance-level aggregates that assign identical QE scores to all N candidates. Consensus-proximity (MBR) converts these to per-sample rankings (§4.3), but these rankings do not improve selection; only sample-specific signals can, in principle, exploit oracle headroom.

**3.2 Confidence Signals**

Four are consistency signals (structural Soft Jaccard [SJ], entity voting confidence [VC]) and surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' κ [FK]); log-probability [LP] is the sole model-internal, per-sample signal.

**Log-probability (model-internal, per-sample).** For sample y_j with tokens t₁, ..., t_L:

σ_lp(y_j) = (1/L) Σᴸₗ₌₁ log p(tₗ | t<ₗ, x)   (1)

**Exact match voting (surface, instance-level).** The proportion of samples producing the most common output:

σ_EM(x) = max_y |{i : yᵢ = y}|/N   (2)

**Fleiss' κ (surface, instance-level).** We adapt Fleiss (1971) to entity sets: items are unique (text, type) tuples across all N samples; each sample assigns binary present/absent labels, yielding a |E_all| × 2 rating matrix.

κ = (P̄ - P̄_e) / (1 - P̄_e)   (3)

where P̄ is mean observed and P̄_e expected agreement. Temperature-based sampling introduces

mild negative dependence (~-0.4% to -4.0%; Appendix B), which does not inflate FK. Unlike structural signals, FK relies on exact string matching.

**Soft Jaccard (structural, instance-level).** For samples y_i, y_j, we group extractions by type, compute max-weight bipartite matching (Hungarian algorithm, token-level IoU), and define:

SJ(yᵢ, yⱼ) = Σₜ sim(uₜ, vₜ) / max(|Uₜ|, |Vₜ|)   (4)

where M is the matched set, sim(uₜ, vₜ) is the token-level IoU between matched spans, and max(|Uₜ|, |Vₜ|) penalizes length asymmetry.¹ The instance-level QE signal averages over all pairs:

σ_sj(x) = Σᵢ<ⱼ SJ(yᵢ, yⱼ) / (N choose 2)   (5)

For selection, σ_sj(x) cannot rank individual candidates (it assigns one score per input). Consensus-proximity converts it to a per-sample score: s_sj(yᵢ) = (1/(N-1)) Σⱼ≠ᵢ SJ(yᵢ, yⱼ), selecting the candidate most consistent with the sample pool, equivalent to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding (Eikema and Aziz, 2022) with SJ as the utility function. The same construction applies to FK, EM, and VC.

**Entity voting confidence (structural, instance-level).** For each entity e in the union E_u of all samples, we compute frequency freq(e) = |{i : e ∈ y_i}|/N. The instance-level confidence is the mean frequency:

σ_vc(x) = (1/|E_u|) Σ_{e∈E_u} freq(e)   (6)

When E_u = ∅, we set σ_vc(x) = 0.²

**3.3 Evaluation Framework**

**Quality estimation.** Spearman ρ between the signal and instance-level F1, and AUROC classifying instances as above/below median F1. Both quality estimation and selection exclude instances with no gold annotations: n=529 on SciERC (from 551), n=2,736 on CoNLL (from 3,453),

**B Robustness Analysis**

We exclude instances with empty gold annotations from all correlation analyses (CoNLL: 4,073/5,453 instances, 20.2%; SciERC: 22851, 4.0%). For these instances, F1 is trivially zero regardless of prediction quality, and consistency signals reflect agreement on the empty set rather than extraction quality, including them inflates or deflates Spearman ρ depending on signal behavior at the boundary.

**Temperature sensitivity.** SF NER ρ shifts from 0.364 (T=0.7) to 0.360 (T=1.0), a difference of 0.004. FK NER ρ drops by 0.022, while RE ρ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced

**[Figure 5: Temperature robustness on SciERC (N=8). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SF maintains stable ρ across T=0.7 and T=1.0, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP shows the largest NER temperature effect (Δρ = 0.014); RE T=0.7 LP data unavailable.]**

diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks. LP exhibits the largest temperature effect on NER (Δρ=0.22) at T=0.7 vs. 0.205 at T=1.0, Δρ=0.014), consistent with lower temperature concentrating probability mass and improving LP's discriminative power for quality estimation. RE T=0/T LP data is not available. Across all comparisons, the signal hierarchy is preserved at both temperatures on NER (SI≈FK>LP at T=0.7: 0.364≈1.0≈0.399≈0.240; at T=1.0: 0.360≈0.267≈0.205).

**Sample size scaling.** Increasing from N=8 to N=16 improves SI on Qwen SciERC NER: ρ rises from 0.360 to 0.411±0.010 (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of ≈0.017. The magnitude of N-scaling gains is setting-dependent: LLaMA SciERC NER yields +0.016 and Qwen CoNLL NER +0.011, though the direction is consistently positive. LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain Δρ=0.012 (range: +0.009 to +0.014) while LP gains only +0.001 (Table 1). FK N-scaling is seed-dependent: Qwen SciERC gains range from +0.005 to +0.023 across seeds (mean seed), while LLaMA CoNLL yields +0.010 (3-seed mean); individual seed FK shifts vary substantially under the unified pipeline, so this should not be interpreted as a robust trend. VC N-scaling is consistently positive (+0.005 on Qwen CoNLL, +0.015 on LLaMA SciERC, +0.030 on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately N-invariant (Δ≤0.003). SI, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows seed-dependent variation that does not constitute a reliable trend, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to N. **FK independence: instance-level permutation test.** To verify that Fleiss' κ reflects genuine within-instance agreement rather than marginal rate artifacts, we conduct instance-level permutation tests across three configurations. For each instance, we permute sample labels 10,000 times to generate a null distribution of FK under independence, then compare the observed FK against this null via a one-sample t-test and permutation p-value.

Table 10 reports the results. All configurations reject the independence null at p<0.001 (n=529–2,756), confirming that FK captures genuine inter-sample agreement rather than chance label co-occurrences. Split-half reliability ranges from r=0.305 (SciERC) to r=0.525 (CoNLL LLaMA), indicating moderate stability: FK estimates from half the samples correlate positively with those from the other half, though the SciERC value sug-

**C Calibration Analysis**

Reliability diagrams use 10 equal-width bins. NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069–0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109–0.339), indicating that translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

**D Additional Analyses**

**Per-relation diagnostic.** RE signal degradation is relation-specific. FEATURE-OF has near-zero correlation (ρ≈0.004), while HYPONYM-OF achieves ρ=0.616. The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5% of RE false negatives, a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions. We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

**Capability stratification.** For NER, SI effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, ρ=0.147, compared to ρ=0.413 for 1-2 entities. The SI advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles (Δρ=0.08–0.14-20). For RE, SI ρ increases monotonically with sentence length (0.21, 0.10 = Q4, 0.473). Filter +set ρ(0.061), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation. Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 (r<0.15), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated (ρ=0.650), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions. For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated (ρ=0.769) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes. ## PAGE 5

**Sample selection.** Best-of-*N* F1: per-sample signals (LP) directly rank candidates; instance-level signals rank via consensus-proximity (MBR utility; see §3 definition above). Baselines: oracle (highest F1 sample) and greedy (*T*=0 single-sample decoding).

**4 Experiments**

**4.1 Experimental Setup**

**Datasets.** We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role. **SciERC** (Luan et al., 2018) (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed where models achieve ≈65% F1. **Few-NERD** (Ding et al., 2021) (INTRA coarse; 37,648 instances, 8 entity types, ≈75% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (§4.4). **CoNLL-2003** (Sang and Meulder, 2003) (3,453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ≈91% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control where limited oracle headroom constrains selection gains. **WNUT-17** (Derczynski et al., 2017) (1,287 social media instances, 52% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.

**Models and sampling.** Both **Qwen3-8B** and **LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct** are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank=32, α=64) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) under identical training procedures. Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint has a minor train–test mismatch (empty thinking tokens); a quantitative analysis rules out this confound (Appendix C). We draw *N*=8 samples at *T*=1.0 (primary), with *N*=16 for scaling experiments.³ Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding (Willard and Louf, 2023).⁴

**4.2 Quality Estimation Results**

Table 1 presents ρ and AUROC for five signals across tasks and models.⁵

**Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent.** On SciERC (medium difficulty), structural signals lead (VC ρ=0.379, SJ 0.360) over surface (ρ≤0.295) and LP (0.205); bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ–LP gap (Δρ=+0.155; Appendix E). On CoNLL (ceiling-effect control, single-sample F1≈0.91), EM leads both ρ and AUROC (0.816); the ρ–AUROC dissociation across datasets reflects use-case alignment. At the signal-collapse boundary—WNUT-17 (macro F1≈42%, 52% zero-F1 instances)—full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary: VC achieves ρ=0.724 (AUROC=0.913) but conditional ρ drops to 0.038 (Table 2). LP shows the reverse pattern (full-set ρ=−0.410, conditional ρ=0.350), confirming that full-set correlations conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation. Restricting to non-zero instances reshuffles rankings, with EM strongest (ρ=0.360; Figure 5).

**4.3 The Correlation-Selection Gap**

We define the correlation-selection gap as the disparity between a signal's instance-level rank correlation with F1 and its ability to select the best output from *N* candidates.

**Table 3:** Best-of-*N* NER selection (macro F1) on SciERC (*N*=8, *T*=1.0, 2-seed mean±σ, *p* vs. greedy baseline from paired sign tests). LP is per-sample; others use consensus-proximity. | *Per-sample signal* | | |
| LP | **0.647** ± 0.005 | .29 |
| *Instance-level signals (consensus-proximity selection)* | | |

Despite moderate quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited selection gains (Table 3, Figure 3). Instance-level signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) assign identical QE scores to all candidates per input; consensus-proximity (MBR) converts these to per-sample rankings (Table 3: SJ 0.646, FK 0.646, EM 0.637, VC 0.623), but none consistently improves over the greedy baseline on the primary test bed. The key question is whether LP—the only natively per-sample signal—can exploit the oracle headroom.

**No significant improvement over greedy.** On SciERC NER (2-seed sign tests⁶, *n*=529), the oracle (0.778) reveals 13.3 pp of headroom above greedy (0.645), yet LP achieves only 0.647 (Δ=+0.2 pp, *p*=0.29); no signal consistently improves selection on SciERC (*p*>0.05; TOST equivalence holds under all external anchors for LLaMA-CoNLL but varies by configuration, Appendix D). The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table 4); RE selection results are consistent (Appendix L). Few-NERD provides a notable exception: LP achieves significant gains (+1.36 pp, *p*<0.001) at low degeneracy, while structural signals still fail (§4.4). CoNLL's near-ceiling single-sample F1 (0.91) with only ~4 pp oracle headroom functions primarily as a ceiling-effect control. Under stringent external TOST anchors (δ₀=1.0 pp), some configurations (e.g., Qwen CoNLL) show statistically significant degradation, indicating signals can actively harm selection (Appendix D). LP approximately matches greedy decoding (*T*=0; Δ=+0.2 pp, not significant); neither significantly outperforms the other, yet both fall far short of the oracle (0.778, 13.3 pp gap). Instance-level signals predict *which inputs* the model handles reliably, not *which output* is best; closing this gap likely requires trained verifiers (Cobbe et al., 2021).⁷

⁶ Multi-seed NER experiments confirm seed variation is small (σ≤0.026; Table 16).

---

## PAGE 7

**4.4 Cross-Dataset Contrast: Few-NERD**

**Table 4:** Cross-dataset comparison of LP selection effectiveness (Qwen3-8B, *N*=8, *T*=1.0). Instance degeneracy monotonically predicts LP selection gains across three datasets. Few-NERD uses gold-filtered evaluation (*n*=32,565); SciERC uses full test set (*n*=551) for protocol consistency.⁸

| Dataset | *n* | Greedy | Headroom | Degen% | LP ρ | LP Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CoNLL | 2,756 | .908 | 4.0 pp | 58% | .316 | fail |
| SciERC | 551 | .614 | 13.8 pp | 21% | .205 | +0.42 pp |
| Few-NERD | 32,565 | .748 | 12.4 pp | 10.1% | .421 | **+1.36** pp |

⁸ SciERC greedy (0.614) and headroom (13.8 pp) differ from Table 3 (gold-filtered *n*=529, greedy=0.645) due to full-set evaluation; the ranking and significance are unchanged.

Few-NERD (Table 4) reveals that instance degeneracy monotonically predicts LP selection effectiveness across datasets. At 10.1% degeneracy (vs. SciERC's 21%, CoNLL's 58%), LP achieves highly significant selection gains (+1.36 pp, 95% CI [+1.18, +1.53], *p*<0.001), while all other signals degrade selection (VC −1.79, SJ −2.14, FK −2.26, EM −3.85 pp).

**Degeneracy as a necessary condition.** Low degeneracy is necessary for LP selection: the cross-dataset gradient is monotonic (58% → fail, 21% → +0.42 pp, 10% → +1.36 pp), and degeneracy below ~15% consistently enables positive LP gains (Figure 2). However, within a dataset, LP signal quality (ρ) provides an additional prerequisite: per-type analysis shows that low degeneracy alone does not guarantee gains (Appendix X). The LoRA-rank ablation (§4.5) corroborates this interaction: reducing rank lowers SciERC degeneracy from 21% to 7% and increases oracle headroom, though LP selection still fails there, confirming that degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient.

**The correlation-selection gap persists for structural signals.** All five signals achieve positive quality estimation on Few-NERD (LP ρ=0.42, VC 0.39, FK 0.31, SJ 0.30, EM 0.29), yet only LP translates QE into selection. The gap between VC's quality estimation (ρ=0.39) and its selection outcome (−1.79 pp) confirms that the gap is not an artifact of weak QE: even strong instance-level QE signals cannot rank candidates within an instance. Within Few-NERD, the degeneracy-gating pattern holds at entity-type granularity: 7 of 8 types show positive LP selection gains (+0.23 to +4.73 pp), while the highest-degeneracy type (Art, 19.8%) is the sole exception (Appendix X).

**Figure 2:** Instance degeneracy vs. LP selection gain. Blue circles: cross-dataset aggregates (CoNLL, SciERC, Few-NERD); orange triangles: per-entity-type within Few-NERD. The dashed line at ~15% separates a regime where LP selection improves over greedy (left) from one where it fails (right). Cross-dataset ordering is monotonic; 7/8 Few-NERD entity types below 20% degeneracy show positive gains. Degeneracy below ~15% appears necessary for LP selection to succeed (Spearman ρ=−0.57, *p*=0.066, *n*=11).

Figure 2 visualizes the relationship across both dataset-level and entity-type-level granularity: degeneracy below ~15% is a necessary condition for LP selection gains.

**LP selection scales with sample budget in the low-degeneracy regime.** On the same 4,351 Few-NERD instances, doubling *N* from 8 to 16 yields a significant additional +0.52 pp (paired bootstrap *p*=0.003, 95% CI [+0.17, +0.87]): LP selection improves from +1.37 pp to +1.88 pp (both *p*<0.001). The gain is driven by reduced degeneracy (11.1% → 4.5%) expanding oracle headroom (12.1 → 15.4 pp), while LP ranking quality remains stable (ρ≈0.62), confirming that signal quality is model-intrinsic rather than *N*-dependent. At *N*=16, all 8 entity types show positive LP gains, including types that were negative at *N*=8. Structural signals remain uniformly negative at *N*=16 (SJ −1.36, FK −1.47 pp), reinforcing that the correlation-selection gap for consensus-based methods persists regardless of sample budget.

**4.5 Robustness**

Consistency signals are robust across *T* ∈ {0.7, 1.0} with sublinear *N*-scaling gains (Table 9); LP shows the largest temperature sensitivity (Δρ=+0.044). Signal rankings are stable across seeds (Kendall's *W*=1.0 at *N*=8; Table 17). NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069–0.096; Appendix G).

**Table 5:** Scale ablation: Qwen3-8B vs. 4B NER quality estimation (ρ; *N*=8, *T*=1.0, seed=42). 8B values identical to Table 1; 4B uses matched evaluation protocol. RE scale ablation in Appendix L.

| | | **8B** | **4B** | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CoNLL | SJ | .436 | .422 | −.014 |
| | FK | .400 | .418 | +.018 |
| SciERC | SJ | .360 | .422 | +.062 |
| | FK | .267 | .326 | +.059 |

**Scale robustness.** Repeating with Qwen3-4B (Table 5), quality estimation is comparable or improved (mean |Δρ|=0.042), yet selection remains below greedy on SciERC (Δ up to −3.4 pp) despite 13.0 pp of oracle headroom, and indistinguishable on CoNLL (<0.3 pp, 1.7 pp headroom). Within the 3B–8B range tested across two model families, task difficulty is a stronger predictor of the gap than model scale; results hold at smaller scale (LLaMA-3.2-3B, 13.6 pp headroom; Appendix V). Instance degeneracy also scales with model capability: 8B shows twice the degeneracy of 4B on SciERC (21% vs. 10.4%) despite comparable within-instance utility correlation (Table 6).

**LoRA-rank ablation.** To disentangle model capacity from degeneracy, we train Qwen3-8B on SciERC with LoRA rank=8 (vs. rank=32 in all other experiments). Reducing rank lowers degeneracy from 21% to 7.2% and increases oracle headroom from 13.3 pp to 16.0 pp, confirming that fine-tuning capacity drives output convergence. How-

---

## PAGE 8

ever, selection still fails: the best signal (LP, 0.635) falls short of greedy (0.640), and all consensus-proximity signals perform worse (SJ 0.631, VC 0.592). Quality estimation remains comparable (VC ρ=0.394 vs. 0.379; SJ ρ=0.365 vs. 0.360). Low degeneracy is thus a necessary but not sufficient condition for selection—LP compression persists regardless of LoRA rank, indicating that both mechanisms must be addressed simultaneously.

**Supervised verifier baseline.** To test whether the information bottleneck lies in the aggregation method or the features themselves, we train a logistic regression verifier on all five signals (3-fold cross-validation on SciERC, *N*=16—giving the verifier access to twice as many samples as the main results). The supervised selector achieves F1=0.641, below both LP (0.647) and greedy (0.644),⁹ closing none of the oracle gap despite the additional samples. Its AUROC (0.652) is lower than single-signal VC (0.706), and feature importance is dominated by VC (coefficient 0.65–0.92) with SJ receiving a negative coefficient. A 2-layer MLP and random forest on the same five features achieve comparable or slightly worse performance (MLP AUROC: 0.639; RF: 0.604), confirming that the bottleneck lies in the feature space rather than the aggregation model. The failure of supervised signal combination confirms that the bottleneck is not in how signals are aggregated but in what information they encode: these features lack per-sample discriminative content sufficient for selection.

⁹ Greedy F1 is 0.644 (3-seed mean in the verifier experiment), consistent with Table 3 (0.645, 2-seed mean on the gold-filtered subset).

**5 Discussion**

**Implications for practitioners.** For quality estimation, all signals achieve positive ρ across non-collapsed datasets (LP ρ=0.42 on Few-NERD, VC ρ=0.38 on SciERC, EM AUROC=0.82 on CoNLL). Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table 5); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse. For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only at low degeneracy: +1.36 pp on Few-NERD (10% degeneracy, *p*<0.001), +0.42 pp on SciERC (21%, *p*=0.091), failure on CoNLL (58%). Structural signals uniformly degrade selection regardless of dataset. RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix L.

**Why the gap exists.** We identify two mechanisms: *instance degeneracy* (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and *LP compression* (affecting per-sample selection).

Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility (Eikema and Aziz, 2022) does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance ρ=0.524 on SciERC, 0.994 on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23% (SciERC) to 41% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap. However, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive *instance degeneracy*: 21% of SciERC instances (58% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all *N* samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13% (49% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table 6). Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value. CoNLL (91% single-sample F1) exhibits 58% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75%) shows 10%; SciERC (66%) shows 21%; WNUT-17 (≈42%, macro) shows near-zero—the tension between model quality and selection utility is inherent, though Few-NERD's low degeneracy despite high performance suggests that dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) also modulate the rate. Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 21% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs. 10.4% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation (ρ=0.52 vs. 0.55; Table 6). Despite MBR's success in machine translation (Freitag et al., 2022), all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix O). On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding (*T*=0; Δ=+0.2 pp, *p*=0.29; Table 3); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 10%, LP achieves significant gains (+1.36 pp, *p*<0.001; Table 4), confirming that degeneracy is the gating factor for LP selection.

Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is severely compressed: median LP range is 0.041 nats (IQR [0.024, 0.073]; Table 18), with pooled within-instance ρ(LP, F1)=0.248 confirming weak but positive signal.

**Non-tied subset analysis.** Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works. Restricting to instances with LP range ≥0.05 (*n*=210, 40% of total; Table 7), within-instance ρ(LP, F1) rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by +2.9 pp (*p*=0.004). The effect grows monotonically with ε (full sweep in Appendix H), and the ε=0.05 result survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons. This demonstrates that LP *does* carry per-sample discriminative information; compression—not signal absence—is the bottleneck. However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset constitutes only 40% of instances, limiting practical impact.

## PAGE 9

**Table 6:** Instance degeneracy statistics (T=1.0, "Constant F1"): all N samples receive identical instance-level F1. "Constant utility": MBR (S0) utility identical across candidates. All data confirms degeneracy scales with model capability.

| Subset | n(LP>F1) | LP ρ | α | τ |

stances with LP range > 0.05 (n=210, 40% of total; Table 7), within-instance ρ(LP, F1) rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by +2.10 pp (p<0.001). The effect grows monotonically with τ (full sweep in Appendix J), and the τ=0.5 result surveys Bonferroni corrections over 5 comparisons. This demonstrates that LP does carry per-sample discriminative information: compression, not signal absence, is the bottleneck. However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset concentrates only 40% of instances, limiting practical impact.

Stratifying by voting confidence reveals a complementary pattern: high-consistency instances (Q4) have collapsed headroom (4.78 pp, leaving nothing to select), while low-consistency instances retain headroom but unreliable LP rankings (Appendix K).

**Effect of sample count.** Increasing N from 2 to 32 expands oracle headroom more than fourfold (+4.4 to +19.2 pp) but yields no commensurate selection improvement. LP selection improves monotonically with N (+0.42 pp at N=6 to +1.01 pp at N=32), but even at N=32, where degeneracy falls to 4% and oracle headroom reaches ~19 pp, the best signal captures less than 5% of the available improvement (Table 20). VC selection degrades with increasing N (−2.27 pp at N=2 to −4.18 pp at N=32), consistent with mode-seeking bias in voting-based selection as the candidate pool grows. Bootstrap significance testing at N=32 (B=10,000) confirms that LP shows a consistent positive trend (+0.95 pp, p=0.031) but does not reach significance at α=0.01; while all signals exceed VC, VC significantly outperforms random selection (p<0.001). Table 30, the gap is not a statistical artifact but a persistent, regime-dependent limitation.

**Effect of sampling temperature.** Oracle headroom increases monotonically with temperature (+7.8 pp at T=0.5 to +13.3 pp at T=1.0), plateauing beyond T=1.0 (+13.0 pp at T=1.2; Table 18 in Appendix), confirming that higher temperature produces more diverse candidate pools. Structural QE signals (SI ρ) improve with temperature: LP ρ vs. greedy|τ (0.297 → 0.371), while LP ρ peaks at T=0.8 (0.253) then degrades, consistent with τ>0.9 compression being model-intrinsic rather than temperature-dependent. Despite expanded headroom and improved QE signals at higher temperatures, selection gains remain negligible, further isolating the bottleneck at the within-instance ranking mechanism rather than signal quality or output diversity.

A verbalized confidence baseline confirms that this compression is not LP-specific: the model's self-rated confidence (mean 8.6/10) is even more compressed and yields the weakest selection despite higher ρ than LP (Appendix U; Bhattacharya et al., 2026). This intrinsic compression extends beyond logprobs; when explicitly prompted to verbalize confidence on a 1-10 scale, models cluster at 8-9 (CoNLL mean 9.24, sd 1.32), exhibiting the same top-biased pattern regardless of output channel.

**Signal combinations.** We test three LP×VC combination strategies: VC-stratified LP selection, LP×VC product ranking, and LP tiebreaking within VC-equivalent groups. All three fail to improve over greedy (best: −0.12 pp, p>0.3), consistent with VC's collapse on degenerate instances and LP's compression on the remainder. An oracle tiebreaker, selecting the highest-F1 sample among VC-equivalent candidates, recovers +7.9 pp, confirming that per-sample signal exists within VC-equivalent groups but current signals cannot extract it.

**Hypotheses for LP compression.** We identify four (non-mutually-exclusive) mechanisms that may explain within-instance LP compression,

---

## PAGE 10

though we do not isolate their individual contributions. Two are *constraint-imposed*: (b) *schema-dominated tokens*, constrained decoding enforces structural tokens (brackets, type labels) that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence, reducing effective variance; (c) *vocabulary saturation*, constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary at each step, concentrating probability mass and reducing log-probability variation. Two are *model-learned*: (a) *token-level averaging*, mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance, compressing the effective signal. (d) *format-token dilution*, fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens ("entities": [ etc.) that carry no extraction information, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens, free-form parse rates of 99.95% confirm that format tokens dominate the sequence.

The constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)-(c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix P), suggesting the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are the primary drivers for NER.

**Ablation: free-form decoding.** Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-3B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix P), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression. Removing formal constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean +2.35 pp (95% CI [+0.42, +4.10], p=0.025, n=397), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level rank rate (sign test: 45%/41%/13.07). Appendix L. More generally, LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard=0.42; Appendix Q), indicating a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode. VC becomes per-sample in the selection context (each candidate's overlap with the majority voted output varies), yet tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias (Eikema and Aziz, 2022; Deguchi et al., 2024). More broadly, all consistency-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table 6; Appendix O).

**Ablation: entity-token LP.** We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation. On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits 4× higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP, confirming that format tokens do compress the signal. However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly worse than full-sequence LP on both datasets (−2.0 pp on SciERC, −3.3 pp on CoNLL). Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction. This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause of LP's selection failure and instead points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope. Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression on CoNLL. 79.4% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP, confirming that compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.

**Pilot remedy.** Entity-token LP projects a natural pilot remedy: if format-token dilution caused compression, restricting LP to entity tokens should recover selection ability. Its failure, particularly the near-zero entity-token variance on CoNLL, suggests that effective remedies must address the underlying model confidence calibration rather than signal aggregation.

**Practical considerations.** Multi-sample inference incurs N× compute cost. For quality estimation, where signals are already reliable (ρ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.42 on the primary test bed; AUROC up to 0.82), N=6 samples suffice (Appendix R), making the cost acceptable for selective prediction or error flagging. For instance-level selection, the cost-benefit is unfavorable: 8× inference yields at most +0.2 pp over greedy (p>0.03). Whether the trade-off shifts in low-convergence regimes (e.g., under-parameterized models where degeneracy drops below 10%) remains an open question.

**Regime boundaries.** The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated. *At the low-resource boundary* (WNUT-17, macro F1≈42%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the

---

## PAGE 11

*trivial-zero boundary* (VC conditional ρ=0.028; Table 2), so selection is moot. *At the ceiling boundary* (CoNLL, F1≈91%, 58% degeneracy), selection shows only a marginal structural exception, VC achieves +0.28 pp (p<0.05) at N=16, capturing ~10% of the 2.5 pp oracle headroom (Appendix R). LP fails entirely. In the *usable-gap regime*, instance degeneracy determines LP effectiveness: at 21% degeneracy (SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant (+0.42 pp, p=0.031); at 10% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains (+1.36 pp, p<0.001; Table 4). This monotonic relationship (58% → full, 21% → weak, 10% → strong) establishes degeneracy as a predictive mechanism, not merely a diagnostic: when candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom. The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Specimen ρ(degen, headroom)=−0.881, p=0.004; Appendix X). Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by consensus, not quality. Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.

**Methodological implications.** The decoupling of ρ, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-source evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal. Even supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLF, random forest) fails to close the oracle gap (§4.5), confirming the information bottleneck is in the features themselves, not the aggregation method. Effective selection thus requires content-aware overlap metrics that examine output semantics (Cobre et al., 2021; Venkateji et al., 2025), not confidence signal aggregation. N>6 captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix R). Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix T).

## 6 Conclusion

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient. All signals achieve reliable quality estimation (ρ up to 0.42 on Few-NERD and SciERC; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging. However, quality estimation does not translate to structural selection: despite 12-14 pp oracle headroom, no structural signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding on any dataset. The gap stems from two jointly operating mechanisms: instance degeneracy (10-58% of instances produce identical F1 across all N samples) and LP compression (median within-instance range of 0.041 nats). Instance degeneracy monotonically predicts LP selection effectiveness across three datasets: at 10% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves +1.36 pp (p<0.001); at 21% (SciERC), LP achieves +0.42 pp (p=0.031); at 58% (CoNLL), LP fails. Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLF, random forest) cannot close the oracle gap, confirming the bottleneck is in the structural feature space. Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open. Closing the structural gap requires content-aware overlap metrics that examine output semantics (Cobre et al., 2021). LP provides a lightweight baseline at low degeneracy.

### Limitations

Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix I, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated. We cover 3B-8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested, larger models may produce more diverse samples. We do not train a verifier, leaving unknown how much oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at N=8 (primary) and N=16; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix R). The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE freeform results are in Appendix L. Qwen3's &lt;think>/&lt;think> ERC checkpoint used empty &lt;think>&lt;/think> blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix H). LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL, tied fractions reach 95.8% at T=0.7); whether reduced temperature translates to selection failures on gains untested. We tested verbalized confidence (Tian et al., 2023) as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.5&/10 on SciERC, 9.25/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix U). Ad-hoc LP×VC combinations yield at most +0.2 pp over greedy (not significant; §5); whether learned combinations could close the gap remains open. The τ=0.05 threshold used for

---

## PAGE 12

tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across τ ∈ [0, 0.2] (Appendix J), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy. We tested one remedy for LP compression, entity-token-only LP (excluding format/schema tokens), which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC (+); LP×VC combinations also fail to recover selection (§5); calibration-based approaches remain unexplored.

### Ethics Statement

All experiments use publicly available benchmarks (SciERC, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17) and open-weight models (Qwen3-3B, Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3.1-8B). CoNLL-2003 is derived from the Reuters RCV1 corpus, which is available for research purposes under a NIST agreement; we use the standard research distribution. No new human data was collected or annotated for this study. Our findings on signal limitations could inform more reliable deployment of IE systems by guiding practitioners toward appropriately confidence signals for their use case. Code and data will be released upon acceptance [anonymized URL].

Despite expanded headroom and improved QE signals at higher temperatures, selection gains remain negligible, further isolating the bottleneck at the within-instance ranking mechanism rather than signal quality or output diversity.\n\nA verbalized confidence baseline confirms that this compression is not LP-specific: the model's self-rated confidence (mean 8.6/10) is even more compressed and yields the weakest selection despite higher ρ than LP (Appendix U; Bhattacharya et al., 2026). Two are *constraint-imposed*: (b) *schema-dominated tokens*, constrained decoding enforces structural tokens (brackets, type labels) that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence, reducing effective variance; (c) *vocabulary saturation*, constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary at each step, concentrating probability mass and reducing log-probability variation. Two are *model-learned*: (a) *token-level averaging*, mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance, compressing the effective signal. (d) *format-token dilution*, fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens (\"entities\": [ etc.) that carry no extraction information, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens, free-form parse rates of 99.95% confirm that format tokens dominate the sequence.\n\nThe constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)-(c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix P), suggesting the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are the primary drivers for NER.\n\n**Ablation: free-form decoding.** Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-3B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix P), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression. Removing formal constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean +2.35 pp (95% CI [+0.42, +4.10], p=0.025, n=397), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level rank rate (sign test: 45%/41%/13.07). Appendix L. More generally, LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard=0.42; Appendix Q), indicating a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode. VC becomes per-sample in the selection context (each candidate's overlap with the majority voted output varies), yet tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias (Eikema and Aziz, 2022; Deguchi et al., 2024). More broadly, all consistency-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table 6; Appendix O).\n\n**Ablation: entity-token LP.** We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation. On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits 4× higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP, confirming that format tokens do compress the signal. However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly worse than full-sequence LP on both datasets (−2.0 pp on SciERC, −3.3 pp on CoNLL). Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction. This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause of LP's selection failure and instead points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope. Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression on CoNLL. 79.4% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP, confirming that compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.\n\n**Pilot remedy.** Entity-token LP projects a natural pilot remedy: if format-token dilution caused compression, restricting LP to entity tokens should recover selection ability. Its failure, particularly the near-zero entity-token variance on CoNLL, suggests that effective remedies must address the underlying model confidence calibration rather than signal aggregation.\n\n**Practical considerations.** Multi-sample inference incurs N× compute cost. For quality estimation, where signals are already reliable (ρ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.42 on the primary test bed; AUROC up to 0.82), N=6 samples suffice (Appendix R), making the cost acceptable for selective prediction or error flagging. For instance-level selection, the cost-benefit is unfavorable: 8× inference yields at most +0.2 pp over greedy (p>0.03). Whether the trade-off shifts in low-convergence regimes (e.g., under-parameterized models where degeneracy drops below 10%) remains an open question.\n\n**Regime boundaries.** The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated. *At the low-resource boundary* (WNUT-17, macro F1≈42%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the\n\n---\n\n## PAGE 11\n\n*trivial-zero boundary* (VC conditional ρ=0.028; Table 2), so selection is moot. *At the ceiling boundary* (CoNLL, F1≈91%, 58% degeneracy), selection shows only a marginal structural exception, VC achieves +0.28 pp (p<0.05) at N=16, capturing ~10% of the 2.5 pp oracle headroom (Appendix R). LP fails entirely. In the *usable-gap regime*, instance degeneracy determines LP effectiveness: at 21% degeneracy (SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant (+0.42 pp, p=0.031); at 10% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains (+1.36 pp, p<0.001; Table 4). This monotonic relationship (58% → full, 21% → weak, 10% → strong) establishes degeneracy as a predictive mechanism, not merely a diagnostic: when candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom. The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Specimen ρ(degen, headroom)=−0.881, p=0.004; Appendix X). Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by consensus, not quality. Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.\n\n**Methodological implications.** The decoupling of ρ, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-source evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal. Even supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLF, random forest) fails to close the oracle gap (§4.5), confirming the information bottleneck is in the features themselves, not the aggregation method. Effective selection thus requires content-aware overlap metrics that examine output semantics (Cobre et al., 2021; Venkateji et al., 2025), not confidence signal aggregation. N>6 captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix R). Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix T).\n\n## 6 Conclusion\n\nWe evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient. All signals achieve reliable quality estimation (ρ up to 0.42 on Few-NERD and SciERC; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging. However, quality estimation does not translate to structural selection: despite 12-14 pp oracle headroom, no structural signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding on any dataset. The gap stems from two jointly operating mechanisms: instance degeneracy (10-58% of instances produce identical F1 across all N samples) and LP compression (median within-instance range of 0.041 nats). Instance degeneracy monotonically predicts LP selection effectiveness across three datasets: at 10% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves +1.36 pp (p<0.001); at 21% (SciERC), LP achieves +0.42 pp (p=0.031); at 58% (CoNLL), LP fails. Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLF, random forest) cannot close the oracle gap, confirming the bottleneck is in the structural feature space. Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open. Closing the structural gap requires content-aware overlap metrics that examine output semantics (Cobre et al., 2021). LP provides a lightweight baseline at low degeneracy.\n\n### Limitations\n\nOur evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix I, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated. We cover 3B-8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested, larger models may produce more diverse samples. We do not train a verifier, leaving unknown how much oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.\n\nWe evaluate at N=8 (primary) and N=16; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix R).
